CausalChain: Metabolic stress in cancer cells -> Altered NSUN2 regulation via post-translational modifications -> Decreased NSUN2 activity and reduced m5C modification on tRNAs -> Increased tRNA susceptibility to angiogenin cleavage -> Accumulation of specific tRNA-derived fragments (tRFs) -> tRFs interact with/displace translation initiation factors and promote ribosome biogenesis -> Selective translation of survival and metabolic adaptation genes -> Enhanced tumor cell survival under metabolic stress
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that metabolic stress in cancer cells initiates a cascade wherein stress-induced post-translational modifications (e.g., phosphorylation or ubiquitination) diminish NSUN2’s methyltransferase activity, leading to a reduction in m5C modification on a subset of tRNAs. The resulting hypomethylated tRNAs are predisposed to angiogenin-mediated cleavage, generating a specific population of tRNA-derived fragments. Uniquely, these tRFs act as molecular switches that bind to and displace key translation initiation factors, and concurrently promote ribosome biogenesis, thereby selectively enhancing the translation of mRNAs encoding proteins critical for cell survival and metabolic adaptation. To substantiate this mechanism, we plan to employ advanced technologies, including high-throughput single-cell RNA sequencing combined with spatial transcriptomics for precise mapping of tRF production, ribosome profiling to monitor shifts in translation, and CRISPR-based perturbations to interrogate NSUN2 regulation and validate the causal roles of these tRFs in reprograming the translational machinery.
Abstract: In response to metabolic stress, cancer cells appear to undergo a multi-layered reprogramming of their epitranscriptomic and translational landscapes. We propose that metabolic stress impairs NSUN2 activity—not solely through diminished expression but also via stress-induced post-translational modifications—resulting in reduced m5C methylation on select tRNAs. These hypomethylated tRNAs become vulnerable to angiogenin-mediated cleavage, yielding a defined subset of tRNA-derived fragments (tRFs). In our model, these tRFs function as regulatory switches by interacting with and displacing specific translation initiation factors, thereby promoting ribosome biogenesis and selectively enhancing the translation of mRNAs linked to survival and metabolic adaptation. We will leverage contemporary single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, and CRISPR-based perturbations to map these events with high resolution, enabling a precise causal dissection of this adaptive mechanism in cancer cells.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis posited that metabolic stress leads to decreased NSUN2-mediated m5C methylation, increased tRNA cleavage by angiogenin, and production of tRFs that displace initiation factors and promote ribosome biogenesis, enhancing translation of survival proteins. The refined hypothesis retains this causal chain but deepens the mechanistic basis by proposing that NSUN2 activity is reduced not only via expression changes but also via stress-induced post-translational modifications. Furthermore, it explicitly outlines the use of high-resolution and spatial technologies (such as single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics) to dissect the process. Each step of the original causal chain is explicitly maintained and expanded upon: (1) metabolic stress alters NSUN2 regulation, (2) leading to decreased m5C marks on tRNAs, (3) which enhances their susceptibility to angiogenin cleavage, (4) resulting in accumulation of specific tRFs, (5) that modulate the translation initiation complex and stimulate ribosome biogenesis, and (6) ultimately facilitate selective translation of genes vital for survival under metabolic stress. This refined model thus offers a more detailed, technologically actionable, and mechanistically nuanced framework.
